results.question: How does the stack work in Magic?

routing.question: How does the stack work in Magic?
routing.wants: How a card or a rule works: timing, the stack, priority, what beats what.
routing.subject: catalogue

results.answer:
What I do not keep is the rules themselves. Timing, the stack, priority, what happens when two things want to happen at once: I will not answer any of those from memory.

What I can do is read you a keyword. Wizards prints the definition of a keyword on the card itself, in brackets, and we hold 208 keywords that way. Ask what flying or hexproof or overload means and you get Wizards' own words back.

For the rest, Gatherer carries the official rulings for a card and the Comprehensive Rules cover everything else. A judge at your local shop will beat both.

results.question: If my creature has deathtouch and trample, how much damage do I have to assign to the blocker?

routing.question: If my creature has deathtouch and trample, how much damage do I have to assign to the blocker?
routing.wants: What a keyword on a card means, in Wizards' own printed words.
routing.subject: catalogue

results.answer:
Each one, in the words Wizards prints on the card:

**Deathtouch**
> Any amount of damage this deals to a creature is enough to destroy it.

**Trample**
> This creature can deal excess combat damage to the player or planeswalker it's attacking.

Those are the reminder texts off Sedge Scorpion and Stampeding Rhino, not something I wrote.

What each one does is above. What happens when they meet is a rule about combat and the order things happen in, and that is the part we do not hold, so I am not going to work it out for you here.

results.question: What happens if I have two legendary creatures with the same name on the battlefield?
results.answer:
I cannot answer that one, and I would rather say so than guess.

Here is what I can settle right now, straight from the catalogue:

- **Pick a card** at the top of the page and I will tell you what it does, what it is legal in, what it costs, what it combos with and whether you already run it.
- **Ask for the most played cards doing a job** and I will list them. Try *best three mana counterspells* or *best removal in black under a dollar*.
- **Ask what a keyword means** and I will read you Wizards' own words off the card. Try *what does hexproof mean* or *what is overload*.
- **Attach a deck** and I will go through its lands and say which slots are weak.

What I do not hold is the rules that are not printed on a card, which is timing, the stack and priority. Nor anything about what is winning at the moment, nor an opinion on whether a card is good.

results.question: What does Rhystic Study do?

routing.question: What does Rhystic Study do?
routing.wants: What a card is, what it does, what it costs and how much it is played.
routing.subject: card

results.answer:
**Rhystic Study** {2}{U}

Enchantment.

What it says, straight off the card:

> Whenever an opponent casts a spell, you may draw a card unless that player pays {1}.

In short: draws cards, taxes the opponent.

We file it under: slows everyone down, draws cards.

Commander plays it at rank 44. That is a place in a list of every card sorted by how many decks run it, so rank 1 is the most played card there is.

It is on the Commander game changer list, which matters for bracket three and below.

Legal in Commander, Legacy, Vintage, Pauper, Brawl, Historic and Oathbreaker. Not legal in Standard, Pioneer and Modern.

About $64.33, or €33.74 in euros. There are 11 printings and they do not all cost the same.

Nothing in the combo list we hold pairs it with anything. That list comes from Commander Spellbook and it is not everything anybody has ever found.

results.answer:
**Cyclonic Rift** {1}{U}

Instant.

What it says, straight off the card:

> Return target nonland permanent you don't control to its owner's hand.
> Overload {6}{U} (You may cast this spell for its overload cost. If you do, change "target" in its text to "each.")

In short: moves cards between zones, has overload.

We file it under: bounces things back to hand, a board wipe.

Commander plays it at rank 54. That is a place in a list of every card sorted by how many decks run it, so rank 1 is the most played card there is.

It is on the Commander game changer list, which matters for bracket three and below.

Legal in Commander, Pioneer, Modern, Legacy, Vintage, Brawl, Historic and Oathbreaker. Not legal in Standard and Pauper.

About $28.45, or €24.40 in euros. There are 15 printings and they do not all cost the same.

It turns up in 16 combos we hold. The 4 most played:

- with Archaeomancer and Brago, King Eternal: lock and return all nonland permanents opponents control to their hand on each of your turns. Needs {6}{U} every turn.
- with Brago, King Eternal and Eternal Witness: lock and return all nonland permanents opponents control to their hand on each of your turns. Needs {6}{U} every turn.
- with Brago, King Eternal and Mnemonic Wall: lock and return all nonland permanents opponents control to their hand on each of your turns. Needs {6}{U} every turn.
- with Brago, King Eternal and Timeless Witness: lock and return all nonland permanents opponents control to their hand on each of your turns. Needs {6}{U} every turn.

When it is good is a table call. We hold what a card does, what it costs and how many decks play it, and none of those add up to that, so I am leaving it to you rather than dressing a guess up as an answer.

results.question: Swords to Plowshares or Path to Exile, which is better?

routing.question: Swords to Plowshares or Path to Exile, which is better?
routing.wants: Two cards side by side, on every number we hold for both.
routing.subject: card

results.answer:
Swords to Plowshares and Path to Exile, side by side. Here is everything we hold about each of them.

**Swords to Plowshares** {W}

Instant.
Exile target creature. Its controller gains life equal to its power.

Commander plays it at rank 11. About $1.34, or €1.52 in euros. Legal in Commander, Legacy, Vintage, Brawl and Oathbreaker. Banned in Historic. Not legal in Standard, Pioneer, Modern and Pauper.

**Path to Exile** {W}

Instant.
Exile target creature. Its controller may search their library for a basic land card, put that card onto the battlefield tapped, then shuffle.

Commander plays it at rank 15. About $1.24, or €1.47 in euros. Legal in Commander, Modern, Legacy, Vintage, Brawl, Historic and Oathbreaker. Not legal in Standard, Pioneer and Pauper.

On the numbers we hold:

- Both cost 1 mana.
- Swords to Plowshares is played more, at rank 11 against 15.
- Path to Exile costs less to buy: $1.24 against $1.34.

Which of two cards is better is a table call. We hold what a card does, what it costs and how many decks play it, and none of those add up to that, so I am leaving it to you rather than dressing a guess up as an answer.

routing.question: What is my win condition in this deck?
routing.wants: How the attached deck actually wins, which is a judgement we do not hold.
routing.subject: deck

results.answer:
How a deck actually wins is a judgement about the list, and I do not hold one. What we store is what each card does and how many decks play it, and neither of those adds up to a plan for closing a game.

Two things near it I can do. Pick a card from the deck and I will give you every combo we hold that it is part of, which is usually where the fast win is. And the deck page works out a power score from the list, which says how quickly it can win without saying how.

results.question: My commander is blue and white. Can I play a card that has a green mana symbol in its rules text?

routing.question: My commander is blue and white. Can I play a card that has a green mana symbol in its rules text?
routing.wants: Whether a mana symbol somewhere on a card counts towards colour identity.
routing.subject: catalogue

results.answer:
Yes it counts, and it is not only the mana cost. A card's colour identity is every mana symbol printed on it, in the cost and in the rules text, and a Commander deck may only play cards whose identity fits inside its commander's.

Here are cards from our own catalogue where that is the whole reason, green in the rules text and nowhere in the cost:

- Talisman of Curiosity costs {2} and its colour identity is green and blue.
- Talisman of Resilience costs {2} and its colour identity is black and green.
- Talisman of Impulse costs {2} and its colour identity is green and red.

So a deck whose commander is not green cannot play Talisman of Curiosity, whatever its cost says.

Two things it does not count. Reminder text in brackets does not, and neither does a colour word written out in letters. A hybrid symbol counts as both of its colours.

results.question: How much commander damage kills a player?
results.answer:
I cannot answer that one, and I would rather say so than guess.

Here is what I can settle right now, straight from the catalogue:

- **Pick a card** at the top of the page and I will tell you what it does, what it is legal in, what it costs, what it combos with and whether you already run it.
- **Ask for the most played cards doing a job** and I will list them. Try *best three mana counterspells* or *best removal in black under a dollar*.
- **Ask what a keyword means** and I will read you Wizards' own words off the card. Try *what does hexproof mean* or *what is overload*.
- **Attach a deck** and I will go through its lands and say which slots are weak.

What I do not hold is the rules that are not printed on a card, which is timing, the stack and priority. Nor anything about what is winning at the moment, nor an opinion on whether a card is good.
